finding.claim: transfer_funds calls check_csrf(), which only returns a boolean, and ignores the result. The CSRF check is never enforced, so a cross-site request can move funds. The function also has other flaws: no validation of the amount (a negative amt reverses the transfer direction and steals from the recipient), no balance check, no authentication check on $_SESSION['uid'], and no transaction, so the two UPDATEs are not atomic.
finding.source: Cross-site forged POST from a malicious page, sent with the victim's session cookie. The attacker controls the amt and to fields, and no valid token is needed. Separately, any authenticated user can submit a negative amt.
finding.sink: UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - ? / bal + ? at actions.php:17-18

trace.note: check_csrf returns a bool and does not exit
return value discarded, so the request proceeds even with a missing or invalid token
debits the session user by the attacker-supplied amt, with no sign, range or balance check

finding.guards_checked: Checked that verify_csrf (line 8), which does exit with a 403, is used in update_profile but not here. SameSite cookie settings are not visible in this code. Prepared statements prevent SQL injection. There is no amount validation, balance check, transaction or login check.

verdict.guard_found: check_csrf (actions.php:4-6) returns a bool but its result is discarded at line 16. verify_csrf (line 8), which exits with 403, is not called here. No SameSite setting, auth check, amount validation, balance check or transaction exists in the directory. Prepared statements only prevent SQL injection.
verdict.reason: actions.php:16 calls check_csrf() as a bare statement, so the request continues to the UPDATEs at actions.php:17-18 whatever the token is. A cross-site forged POST can therefore move funds, and a negative amt reverses the transfer direction.
